title: Off Center
subtitle: A crooked nose that will not breathe, from the basal view to the last suture
description: Reading the caudal septum on examination, choosing the right facial midline, deciding what imaging adds, repositioning the caudal septum, the bony vault, the cartilaginous dorsum, and the tip and columella.

steps.title: Step 1/7: The Basal View
steps.scenario:
A 27-year-old woman comes in for a nose that is blocked on the right and, she says, has never looked straight. No trauma she remembers. No prior nasal surgery. Intranasal steroid for three months did nothing.

On anterior rhinoscopy the caudal end of the septum sits in the right vestibule, well off the midline. The columella leans right and the right nostril is narrower than the left. Pressing the right cheek laterally opens the airway a little; lifting the right ala opens it a lot.
steps.media: Load image: Basal view photograph, consented, unannotated: caudal septum dislocated into the right vestibule, columella tilted right, asymmetric nostrils. Caption: 'Basal view.'
steps.question: What is the primary cause of her right-sided obstruction?

options.text: (A) Right inferior turbinate hypertrophy
(B) Caudal septal deviation, with the septum dislocated off the anterior nasal spine into the right vestibule
(C) Internal nasal valve collapse from a narrow angle between the upper lateral cartilage and the septum
(D) External valve collapse from a weak lateral crus

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The caudal septum is the part you can see without an endoscope, and here it is sitting in the right vestibule instead of on the anterior nasal spine. That is a dislocation, not a bend. It narrows the right nostril directly, pushes the columella to the right, and because the medial crura sit on it, it drags the tip off center too. The intranasal steroid was never going to move cartilage.

The two maneuvers tell you where the block is. A modified Cottle, lifting the ala with a probe, opens the vestibule and the caudal septum: a large improvement means the problem is at the front. A classic Cottle, pulling the cheek laterally, opens the internal valve: a small improvement means the internal valve is not the main issue.

Why the others fail:
(A) The turbinate on the wider left side may be compensating, but you can see the caudal septum filling the right vestibule. The turbinate is not what she feels.
(C) The internal valve is further back, at the angle between the upper lateral cartilage and the dorsal septum. A weak response to the classic Cottle argues against it. It may need attention later, but it is not the primary cause.
(D) External valve collapse means the ala falls in on inspiration. Hers does not. The vestibule is narrowed by septal cartilage, not by a floppy lateral crus.

Keypoint: a caudal septum you can see in the vestibule is a structural problem, and a big response to lifting the ala tells you the block is at the front.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Clinical consensus statement: septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Rhee JS, Poetker DM, Smith TL, et al. Nasal valve surgery improves disease-specific quality of life. Laryngoscope. 2005;115(3):437-440.

steps.title: Step 2/7: Which Midline
steps.scenario:
On the frontal photograph the whole nose leans to the right. But her chin also sits to the left of center, and her right midface is shorter than her left.

You are planning how far to move the nose.
steps.media: Load image: Frontal photograph, consented, with three lines drawn in your own software: mid-glabella to mid-Cupid's bow, mid-glabella to chin point, and the current nasal axis. Caption: 'Which line.'
steps.question: Which line do you align the nose to?

options.text: (A) Mid-glabella to the chin point
(B) Halfway between the chin line and the Cupid's bow line, as a compromise
(C) The current nasal axis, moved only enough to straighten the dorsum on itself
(D) Mid-glabella to mid-Cupid's bow, ignoring the chin

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

In a patient with facial asymmetry, the chin is not a reliable midline landmark. In a prospective series of 100 rhinoplasty patients, nasal deviation had no correlation with chin deviation, and aligning the nose to a deviated chin produced a nose that looked wrong on an otherwise centered upper face. The line that works is mid-glabella to mid-Cupid's bow, which stays close to the true facial midline even when the chin and lower face are off. The same series found the nasal bones most often deviated toward the shorter side of the midface, which fits her: right midface short, nose to the right.

Why the others fail:
(A) The chin is deviated. Aligning to it moves the nose to a line that is itself off center.
(B) A compromise between a correct reference and a wrong one is still partly wrong. Pick the landmark that is reliable.
(C) Straightening the dorsum on its own axis leaves the whole nose leaning. Her complaint is that it has never looked straight, and that means the axis, not just the dorsum.

Keypoint: in an asymmetric face, align the nose from mid-glabella to mid-Cupid's bow, and expect the nasal bones to have drifted toward the short side.

Reference: Farkas LG, Hreczko TA, Kolar JC, Munro IR. Vertical and horizontal proportions of the face in young adult North American Caucasians. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1985;75(3):328-338. Facial asymmetry and nasal axis series (prospective, N=100) and nasal bone deviation pattern study (N=76), as presented in the 2025-07-03 rhinoplasty journal reading; complete both citations from the reading list.

steps.title: Step 3/7: What Imaging Adds
steps.scenario:
You are planning an open septorhinoplasty. The septum will need strong support once it is repositioned, and you are considering a bony batten from the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid.

She asks whether she needs a CT.
steps.question: What do you tell her about imaging?

options.text: (A) CT is not needed for the septal diagnosis; it may help here to check ethmoid plate thickness for a bony batten and to rule out sinus disease
(B) CT is required to confirm and grade the septal deviation before surgery
(C) No imaging of any kind is ever indicated before septorhinoplasty
(D) MRI, to assess the cartilage

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The AAO-HNSF consensus statement on septoplasty is explicit: CT may not accurately demonstrate the degree of septal deviation. The diagnosis is made on anterior rhinoscopy and endoscopy, and she already has it. Where CT earns a place is for what it shows that the examination cannot. If you plan to harvest a bony batten from the perpendicular plate, the plate needs to be thick enough to survive the harvest: the PPE split series used a threshold of 3 mm on preoperative CT, and even then about one graft in eight fractured. And if there is any suggestion of chronic sinus disease, the scan answers that before you commit to an airway operation.

Why the others fail:
(B) The consensus statement says the opposite. A CT can under-read or over-read a caudal deviation, and it adds nothing to what you saw in the vestibule.
(C) Too absolute. Imaging is not required for the septum, but it can be useful for graft planning and sinus assessment.
(D) MRI does not show bone, which is what you are planning to harvest, and it has no role in assessing septal cartilage for surgery.

Keypoint: the septum is diagnosed by looking; CT is for planning bone grafts and excluding sinus disease.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Clinical consensus statement: septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Kim D, Nam SH, Al-harethy S, et al. Surgical outcomes of bony batten to correct caudal septal deviation in septoplasty. JAMA Facial Plast Surg. 2017;19(6):470-475. PPE split technique series (36 patients, PPE thickness over 3 mm on CT, 12 percent graft breakage): PMID 39138596; complete the citation.

steps.title: Step 4/7: The Caudal Septum
steps.scenario: Open approach. The caudal septum is dislocated to the right of the anterior nasal spine, and the cartilage is thin. You have a 1.5 cm dorsal and caudal L-strut to preserve.
steps.media: Load image: Intraoperative photograph, open approach, unannotated: caudal septum seen lying to the right of the anterior nasal spine. Caption: 'Caudal septum, open.'
steps.question: How do you correct it?

options.text: (A) Resect the dislocated caudal centimeter and close
(B) Score the concave side of the caudal septum until it straightens
(C) Free the caudal septum from the spine, swing it back to the midline, fix it to the periosteum of the spine, and splint it with a batten or an extension graft
(D) Leave the caudal septum and reduce the right inferior turbinate instead

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

The caudal septum is the foundation. It holds the tip up, it sets the columella, and the medial crura rest on it. The correction is to release it from its wrong position, reposition it over the anterior nasal spine on the side you chose in Step 2, suture it down to the periosteum so it cannot swing back, and then give it something rigid to lean on. In a thin Asian septum that support comes from a batten, and a bony batten from the perpendicular plate is the strongest option when the plate is thick enough. When septal cartilage is short, folded cymba concha is a reliable alternative for a caudal extension graft. If the septum still needs length or the tip needs projection, a caudal septal extension graft does both jobs at once, and it does not matter which side you put it on: in 122 patients, graft laterality made no difference to postoperative tip symmetry.

Why the others fail:
(A) Resecting the caudal septum removes the tip's support. The tip drops, the columella retracts, and you have created a saddle and a revision. The caudal strut is preserved, not resected.
(B) Scoring weakens cartilage that is already thin, and cartilage memory pulls it back over months. The move is to redirect and splint, not to force.
(D) The turbinate is on the other side and is not what she feels. Reducing it does nothing for a septum sitting in the right vestibule.

Keypoint: release, reposition to the spine, suture to periosteum, splint with bone or a graft; never resect the caudal strut.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Clinical consensus statement: septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Gubisch W. Twenty-five years experience with extracorporeal septoplasty. Facial Plast Surg. 2006;22(4):230-239. Chung YS, Seol JH, Choi JM, et al. How to resolve the caudal septal deviation? Clinical outcomes after septoplasty with bony batten grafting. Laryngoscope. 2014;124(8):1771-1776. Kim D, Nam SH, Al-harethy S, et al. Surgical outcomes of bony batten to correct caudal septal deviation in septoplasty. JAMA Facial Plast Surg. 2017;19(6):470-475. CSEG laterality and tip symmetry series (122 patients) and folded cymba concha as a CSEG alternative, as presented in the 2025-04-09 structural grafting journal reading; complete the citations.

steps.title: Step 5/7: The Bony Vault
steps.scenario: The nasal bones lean to the right. On the frontal photograph the rhinion sits 3 mm to the right of the midline you chose. The right sidewall is concave, the left convex. Her nasal bones are short and thin, and you plan to augment the dorsum afterward.
steps.question: What do you do to the bony vault?

options.text: (A) Bilateral medial and lateral osteotomies, as for a hump reduction
(B) No osteotomy; the bony deviation is too small to matter
(C) A one-unit osteotomy, mobilizing the whole pyramid to rotate it to the midline
(D) A selective osteotomy on the concave side with rasping, preserving the keystone and a wide dorsal platform

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The selective osteotomy protocol starts with one number: rhinion displacement, the distance from the rhinion to the midline. Five millimeters or less, and the bony vault can be corrected with a unilateral osteotomy on the concave side, with or without rasping of the convex side, without opening the keystone. More than 5 mm needs bilateral or conventional osteotomies. Hers is 3 mm. In the original series this approach achieved objective correction in 88 percent and satisfaction in 98 percent, with no collapse or revision.

The reason to be conservative is her anatomy and her plan. Asian nasal bones are short, thin and low, and they do not tolerate aggressive mobilization. And you are going to augment the dorsum: a slightly wider, stronger bony platform supports the graft and keeps the dorsal lines. That is the opposite of the Western hump-reduction habit of narrowing the vault as much as possible.

Why the others fail:
(A) Bilateral medial and lateral osteotomies are the hump-reduction toolkit for a high dorsum with strong bones. On her bones they risk collapse, irregularity, and a vault too narrow to carry the augmentation.
(B) Three millimeters of rhinion displacement is visible, and she came because the nose looks crooked. Leaving it means the dorsum you build on top will lean too.
(C) The one-unit osteotomy mobilizes the whole pyramid as a block and is designed for asymmetric bone length, an oblique or rotated pyramid, or facial asymmetry with axis deviation beyond what a selective cut can fix. It works, and in 20 patients it improved deviation from 6.9 to 2.1 degrees, but it is more than she needs.

Keypoint: measure the rhinion displacement; 5 mm or less, selective unilateral osteotomy and keep the keystone.

Reference: Selective osteotomy protocol (Kang, 2018; rhinion displacement 5 mm cutoff, 88 percent objective correction, 98 percent satisfaction) and one-unit osteotomy series (Kim, 2022; 20 patients, deviation 6.9 to 2.1 degrees), as presented in the 2025-07-03 rhinoplasty journal reading. Verify both against the original papers before use; the figures here are taken from the slides.

steps.title: Step 6/7: The Cartilaginous Dorsum
steps.scenario: With the caudal septum reset and the bones moved, the cartilaginous dorsum still curves to the right. The dorsal septum is off center at the anterior septal angle, and the upper lateral cartilage on the right is narrower than the left.
steps.media: Load image: Intraoperative photograph, open approach, unannotated: a unilateral extended spreader graft on the concave side alongside a caudal septal extension graft. Caption: 'New center.'
steps.question: How do you straighten it?

options.text: (A) A unilateral extended spreader graft on the concave side, fixed to a caudal septal extension graft that sets a new midline
(B) Bilateral symmetric spreader grafts
(C) Cross-hatch the dorsal septum on the convex side until it lies flat
(D) Reduce the dorsal hump to take the curve out

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Symmetric techniques assume the septum is already central. Hers is not. The approach that works when the structural midline is displaced is to build a new one: a caudal septal extension graft is fixed where the midline should be, and a single extended spreader graft on the concave side splints the dorsal septum to it. The graft does not force the cartilage straight; it redirects the load so that cartilage memory works with you instead of against you. The L-strut stays intact, which keeps the revision options open. In the original series this corrected the dorsal deviation angle by 3.7 degrees toward the midline, increased tip projection by 7 percent, and reduced nostril axis inclination by 11.7 degrees, all significant.

Why the others fail:
(B) Bilateral spreaders widen the middle vault symmetrically around whatever midline the septum already has. If that midline is to the right, the dorsum stays to the right, only wider.
(C) Cross-hatching weakens the dorsal strut, the part of the L-strut you most need, and thin Asian cartilage weakened on one side tends to warp again. It also does nothing to relocate the midline.
(D) There is no hump. Reducing the dorsum on a curved septum removes height and leaves the curve.

Keypoint: when the midline itself is displaced, build a new one with an extension graft and splint to it with a unilateral spreader; do not force symmetric grafts onto an asymmetric septum.

Reference: Chen YY, Kim SA, Jang YJ. Centering a deviated nose by caudal septal extension graft and unilaterally extended spreader grafts. Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol. 2020;129(5):448-455. doi:10.1177/0003489419894617.

steps.title: Step 7/7: The Tip and the Columella
steps.scenario: The dorsum is now straight on the line you chose. But looking from below, the columella still leans right, the right medial crus sits lower than the left, and the right nostril is still narrower.
steps.media: Load image: Intraoperative basal view, unannotated, before tip work: straight dorsum, columella still deviated, asymmetric nostrils. Caption: 'Before the tip.'
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: (A) Accept it; the dorsum is straight and the airway is open, which is what she came for
(B) Another osteotomy to bring the columella across
(C) Straighten the medial crura on a columellar strut or the extension graft, equalize their height, and correct the lateral crura where they differ
(D) Alar base reduction on the wider side

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

This is the part that gets skipped, and it is the part patients look at. A crooked nose operation that leaves the columella leaning and the nostrils uneven feels wrong to the patient even when the dorsum is perfect, because people judge a nose from the front and from below by the tip and the nostrils. The dislocated caudal septum has pushed the medial crura apart and twisted them; the deviated upper lateral cartilage has pushed one lateral crus out. So you fix the lower third on its own terms. Suture the medial crura to a columellar strut or to the extension graft so they sit side by side at the same height. Where a lateral crus is longer, shorten it with a cut-and-overlap suture; where it buckles, a concavity control suture. Clocking sutures rotate the tip complex onto the new midline. A rim graft supports a retracted ala.

At six months her NOSE score fell from 16 to 4, and the basal view shows a centered columella and matching nostrils.

Why the others fail:
(A) The airway is only half the complaint. She said the nose has never looked straight, and a leaning columella is what she will see in the mirror. Correcting the bone and septum alone produces high dissatisfaction rates.
(B) The bones are done. The columella is held by the medial crura, not by the nasal bones, and another osteotomy would only destabilize the vault.
(D) Alar base reduction changes nostril width at the sill. It does not straighten a columella or level the medial crura, and doing it before the crura are fixed sets the asymmetry in place.

Keypoint: a straight dorsum is not a finished nose; fix the medial crura, the lateral crura, and the columella, because that is what the patient sees.

Reference: Gruber RP, Nahai F, Bogdan MA, Friedman GD. Changing the convexity and concavity of nasal cartilages and cartilage grafts with horizontal mattress sutures. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2005;115(2):595-606. Stewart MG, Smith TL, Weaver EM, et al. Outcomes after nasal septoplasty: results from the Nasal Obstruction Septoplasty Effectiveness (NOSE) study. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2004;130(3):283-290. Lower nasal vault correction series (Suh MK, 2020), as presented in the 2025-07-03 rhinoplasty journal reading; complete the citation.
